Hearken
HARK-en
v.
From Old English heorcnian, an intensive of hīeran (to hear)—to listen attentively, give heed. Renders the Hebrew shāma, “to hear so as to obey,” the keynote verb of Israel’s confession (Shema Yisrael), and the Greek akouō, “to hear.”

📖 Biblical Definition

To hearken is to hear with the will engaged—to listen with a view to obeying, not merely to register sound. Scripture treats the ear as a moral organ: God’s controversy with His people is not that they have not heard, but that they have not hearkened, have not bowed the will to what the ear received. Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God is one LORD is no abstract proposition; it is a summons to ordered obedience. The whole Old Testament can be read as God’s pleading with a people who hear and do not hearken: they have ears, but they hear not; since the day that your fathers came forth out of the land of Egypt unto this day I have even sent unto you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them: Yet they hearkened not unto me. Hearkening is the inner motion that translates revelation into obedience. It is what Mary did when she said be it unto me according to thy word; it is what Samuel learned when he answered speak; for thy servant heareth; it is what the wise man does who, hearing his father’s instruction, performs it; and it is what the foolish man refuses. To hearken is therefore the first act of faith and the chief act of the disciple: the ear that hears and the heart that yields. The mark of the sheep, Christ said, is precisely this: my sheep hear my voice, and they follow me—hearing fused with following, hearkening as the inner shape of discipleship.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines HEARKEN as to listen; to lend the ear; to attend to what is uttered, with eagerness or curiosity; hence, in scripture, to hear with attention and obey.

expand to see more

HEARKEN, v.i. — 1. To listen; to lend the ear; to attend to what is uttered, with eagerness or curiosity; as, to hearken to a story or a lecture. 2. In scripture, to attend with submission or obedience; to obey; as, to hearken to the voice of the Lord; the people would not hearken to the prophet.

HEARKENING, ppr. — Listening; attending to; obeying.

📖 Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 6:4 — "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD."

1 Samuel 15:22 — "Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams."

Jeremiah 7:25-26 — "Since the day that your fathers came forth out of the land of Egypt unto this day I have even sent unto you all my servants the prophets... Yet they hearkened not unto me, nor inclined their ear, but hardened their neck."

John 10:27 — "My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Hearkening is corrupted by the listening culture that mistakes the registering of words for the bowing of the will—the podcast-and-sermon-consuming age that hears more, retains more, and obeys less than any generation that has come before it.

expand to see more

Never has more religious teaching reached the ear of the church, and never has the ear been less a moral organ. The believer of the present age has access to the world’s great preachers on demand, can consume sermons by the hour while driving, may sit under more careful exposition in a week than the medieval saint heard in a lifetime—and yet the practical obedience of the same believer is often visibly thinner than that of his unlettered forebears. The breakdown is at hearkening. The age has trained the ear to hear without bowing the will; sermons are taken as content to evaluate, not as the voice of God to obey; the very abundance of teaching cultivates the posture of the consumer, who samples and rates and moves on, rather than the posture of the disciple, who hears in order to do.

Scripture’s rebuke is sharp: be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. The hearer-only is a man who looks at his face in a mirror and forthwith forgets what manner of man he was; the hearkener is the man who, having heard, goes and does. Recover the doctrine that the ear is a moral organ, that to hear is to be obligated, that God speaks not to inform but to command, and that the sheep of His pasture are known not by how much teaching they consume but by how readily they follow the Shepherd’s voice—and the consumer-listener is reformed back into the disciple-hearkener God means His sheep to be.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shāma (to hear so as to obey)—the verb of the Shema—and Greek akouō (to hear, often with obedience implied), with hupakouō as the explicit hear-under, obey.

expand to see more

Hebrew shāma (H8085) — to hear, listen, obey; the keynote verb of the Shema in Deut 6:4.

Greek akouō (G191) — to hear, to listen, sometimes with implicit obedience.

Greek hupakouō (G5219) — to hear-under, to obey (the fused form makes the relation explicit).

Hebrew qāshab (H7181) — to incline the ear, attend carefully—the posture-of-the-ear word.

Usage

"Hearkening is hearing with the will engaged—the ear that bows the soul, not merely registers sound."

"To obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams—Samuel’s rebuke is still the standard."

"The age consumes more teaching than any before and hearkens to it less—the ear is a moral organ, and ours has been numbed."
